masthead_title: Every Treasury tenor flags at once and the 10-year hits a fresh cycle high, but investment-grade credit doesn't blink — and two AI-adjacent stocks post the same selloff in opposite directions
provenance_note: Stated reasons and press framing via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): CNBC, The Motley Fool, Yahoo Finance, Seeking Alpha, Benzinga, MarketBeat, TradingKey, 24/7 Wall St., Trading Strategy Guides, the World Economic Forum. No paid services used (Bigdata.com removed 2026-08-21).
regime_line: The whole Treasury curve sold off together overnight into Wednesday's close — 3-month, 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year all now sit higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months (§4, |z| ≥ 1.5) — pushing the 10-year to 4.83%, this system's highest recorded close, while the credit market that would normally flag real financial stress stayed almost perfectly calm.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — four claims resolve this morning, one new one opens

Four open claims hit or passed their deadline overnight; all are reconciled against Wednesday's data before anything new is written (§4B). Yesterday is answered before today is asserted.

  • CL-0008 — confirmed. The claim: Monday 09-01's California wildfire-liability selloff in Edison International and PG&E was a state-specific regulatory shock, not the start of broader credit stress. Test: IG OAS (the extra yield investors demand to lend to investment-grade companies) stay at or below 0.84% through today. It never left 0.81% the entire window (08-28 base was 0.79%), comfortably inside the cap. No sign the story spread into broader investment-grade credit.
  • CL-0009 — expired, reported plainly. The claim: last week's software/cybersecurity selloff was rate-driven, not sector-specific. The test needed both halves to move together — UST 10Y staying ≥ 4.70% and SMH (the semiconductor fund this system uses as a growth-stock proxy) underperforming SPY by ≥ 1 additional point. The rate half held — 10Y kept climbing, to this morning's 4.83% — but SMH did the opposite of "worsen": it's now running 4.7 percentage points ahead of SPY since the 09-02 baseline (SMH +4.3%, SPY −0.4%). The refute wording never fired either, since it required 10Y to fall below 4.70%, which didn't happen. Neither box fits as written — rates kept rising while the growth-stock complex firmly recovered, which argues against a simple "rates are the whole story" read, but the test itself didn't anticipate that combination. Expired unresolved at its own deadline rather than forced to a verdict the data doesn't support.
  • CL-0010 — expired unresolved, exactly as designed. The claim tested whether the blowout August payrolls report would push the 2-year decisively past 4.40% (reversal) or hold below 4.30% (dovish repricing survives), with the 4.30–4.40% band itself labeled inconclusive up front. The 2-year printed 4.37% on 09-04 and 4.39% on Monday 09-08 — inside that band both times. This is the one claim this morning whose "no result" is itself the result the test was built to allow.
  • CL-0012 — confirmed. The claim: Friday's muted 10-year close (+1bp) despite a payrolls beat ~2.8x consensus meant the surprise was priced in beforehand, not a reaction hidden behind this system's one-day-lagged real-yield data. Tuesday 09-08's TIPS real-yield fill (which carries the actual 09-04 print, once the lag caught up) came in at 2.43%, up just 1 basis point from Thursday 09-03's 2.42% base — well under the 3bp bar for "priced in," nowhere near the 5bp bar that would have said "real move, just lagged." Confirmed.
  • CL-0011 — still open (due tomorrow, 09-11). Testing whether Ciena's in-line guidance signals a broader AI-networking slowdown. SMH remains far outside the refute band (now +4.7pp vs. SPY since the 09-03 baseline, not the ≤1pp the refute condition specifies) — leaning toward "Ciena-specific," graded tomorrow.

One new conditional claim opens this morning. CL-0013 — today's whole-curve selloff has at least three competing press explanations (below); this morning's Core PPI release (due after this data pull, consensus +0.3% m/m) and tomorrow's lagged real-yield/breakeven fill are the test. A hot Core PPI (≥ 0.4% m/m) paired with the 09-10-dated breakeven rising ≥ 3bp from Tuesday's 2.37% base would support an inflation/term-premium read; an in-line-or-cooler PPI (≤ 0.2% m/m) paired with the real-yield component still climbing while breakeven stays flat or lower would instead point to a growth/real-rate story. Default 5-trading-day window, due 2026-09-17 — likely gradable sooner, as soon as the lagged fill lands.
story_html:
Wednesday's press coverage led almost entirely with the bond market. Trading Strategy Guides' own recap was headlined "Yield Spike Sinks Stocks"; CNBC and the World Economic Forum both carried pieces this week arguing the bond selloff reflects rekindled inflation fear — pointing to elevated oil prices tied to the ongoing Iran-related tensions this system logged and tested back on 08-31 (CL-0007, confirmed), plus reports that heavy new corporate bond issuance from AI companies (a figure north of $1.5 trillion that this system first flagged, Bloomberg-sourced, on 09-03) is crowding out demand for Treasuries. Other coverage pointed to reported Bank of Japan-linked selling of U.S. Treasuries to help defend the yen. One press figure this system can't corroborate: several outlets described oil as trading "above $100"; this system's own script-verified WTI print (Yahoo CL=F) has it at $96.05 Wednesday, up sharply on the day (+3.2%) and up from the high-$80s a week ago, but not above $100 — flagged here as a discrepancy rather than silently adopted (§4C).

Does the state file confirm the inflation-fear story? Only partially, and credit is the detail that matters most. The rate move itself is real and system-verified: the 10-year rose 3bp to 4.83% — its highest close in this system's history — and every single Tier 1 Treasury tenor this system tracks (3-month, 2-year, 10-year, 30-year) is now flagged (§4, |z| ≥ 1.5), meaning each sits higher than on all but a handful of days in the past six months. That's a genuine, broad-based move, not a headline exaggerating a small one. But the piece of the puzzle that would actually confirm "inflation fear" specifically — credit spreads, the market's own read on default and liquidity risk — didn't move that way at all. High-yield spreads (the extra yield junk-rated borrowers pay over Treasuries) eased to 2.67%, still below its own six-month average (z −0.82); investment-grade spreads held flat at 0.81%, confirming CL-0008 above. If bond investors were genuinely pricing rising inflation or credit risk, spreads are usually among the first places it shows up — and they haven't moved. The one series that would settle this cleanly — the real-yield/breakeven split (Unit 2's toolkit) — is one day behind, dated Tuesday 09-08, and doesn't yet include Wednesday's move; that's the same lag that produced last Monday's capstone lesson, replayed here as this morning's new claim (CL-0013, above), with today's Core PPI print as the first real test. Underneath the rate story, Wednesday also produced a genuine split inside the AI trade itself — see Movers, below — which argues today isn't a single, monolithic "AI capex" signal either.
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail Wednesday's 2026-09-09 close: TIPS real yield, breakeven, both credit-spread series, and SOFR publish a day behind (§5), dated Tuesday 09-08 (the standard lag, widened slightly this week by Monday's Labor Day closure). Fed balance sheet and TGA are the weekly Thursday H.4.1 release, still dated to last week. Treasury tenors (3m/2y/10y/30y) and equities are same-day fresh via Treasury.gov and Yahoo, cross-checked against FRED's next-day figures. Flagged rows (⚑): higher (or lower) than on all but a handful of days in the past six months — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: The whole curve moved, and it moved together. The 3-month rose 1bp to 3.95% (z +1.85), the 2-year rose 4bp to 4.43% (z +1.99), the 10-year rose 3bp to 4.83% (z +2.14, the largest flag on today's board), and the 30-year rose 3bp to 5.28% (z +1.82) — every Tier 1 Treasury series this system tracks is now flagged. In real terms: anyone with a mortgage rate lock coming up, a money-market fund, a CD renewing, or a bond fund in a client account is pricing off the most expensive borrowing curve this system has recorded since it started keeping score. The curve's shape moved in two directions at once, worth naming carefully: 2s10s (the gap between 2-year and 10-year yields, a classic recession/expectations gauge) narrowed 1bp to 40bp as the 2-year rose faster than the 10-year, while the 3-month-to-10-year spread widened 2bp to 88bp (z +1.56, flagged) as the 10-year outran the 3-month — a reminder that "the curve" isn't one number; different parts of it can tell slightly different stories on the same day. Credit stayed the calm outlier. High-yield spreads eased to 2.67% (z −0.82, below its own six-month average) and investment-grade spreads held flat at 0.81% (z +0.59) — both dated Tuesday — meaning the market that prices default and liquidity risk isn't pricing any extra fear, even as the "risk-free" curve got measurably more expensive. That gap between a stressed-looking rate move and an unstressed credit market is exactly what keeps this morning's regime tag at "tightening" rather than "stress" (today's concept, below, is built around this exact distinction). The real-yield/breakeven decomposition that would show whether Wednesday's move was growth-driven or inflation-driven is still dated Tuesday 09-08 (real yield 2.43%, z +1.33; breakeven 2.37%, z +0.50) — one day behind, so it doesn't yet include Wednesday's move (see CL-0013, above). Breadth was weaker than the headline index: the equal-weight S&P proxy (RSP) fell 0.97% against cap-weight SPY's 0.47% decline, and the Russell 2000 (−1.32%) sold off harder than the S&P 500 (−0.49%) — smaller, more rate-sensitive names bore more of Wednesday's pressure than the mega-caps that dominate the headline index. Copper (z +1.69, flagged) and gold (+0.5% on the day but barely above its own average, z +0.01) both firmed — gold's rise without a matching z-flag is itself informative: this has been a gradual multi-week climb, not a single-day flight to safety. Dollar index (DXY) eased slightly (−0.07 to 98.77, z −0.88) despite the broad rate rise — a genuine curiosity given Unit 5's not-yet-reached lesson that higher U.S. yields usually pull the dollar up via rate differentials; reported plainly as an open question rather than explained away, since this system doesn't yet have a EUR/USD or USD/JPY series to test the reported yen-defense story directly.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 25 name candidates and 0 sector divergences qualified Wednesday; cap is 3 names + a sector note (omitted today — no GICS sector ETF cleared the 1.5pp mechanical threshold, though Charter Communications and Comcast both fell 6-8% on broadband-specific news, not enough to move their sector as a whole).

CASY −14.24% (629.03, from 733.49) — what happened: Casey's General Stores' sharpest one-day drop in years, despite beating estimates. Stated reason: Yahoo Finance, Benzinga, and Seeking Alpha report Casey's fiscal Q1 (ended July 31) beat on revenue ($5.68B vs. $5.57B consensus) and earnings, but inside same-store sales growth of 3.2% came in below elevated investor expectations, and the stock carried a premium valuation into the print — a "sell the news" reaction rather than a results problem. Why it matters: a third consecutive instance this system has tracked (after Walmart, CL-0004 confirmed, and Lululemon on 09-07) of a consumer-facing name being punished for decelerating growth even where the headline numbers were fine — worth watching as a pattern rather than three isolated stories (§8 wall applies: no view offered on the stock's investment merit).

VRT −9.61% (262.89, from 290.83) — what happened: Vertiv's steepest pullback in months. Stated reason: MarketBeat, TradingKey, and Trefis report broad profit-taking across AI-datacenter power and cooling infrastructure stocks after a prolonged multi-quarter run, with valuation scrutiny intensifying rather than any reported change to hyperscaler capex plans or order backlogs. Why it matters: a genuine AI-capex-adjacent name selling off hard on the same day the discount-rate curve (see dashboard, above) moved sharply higher — consistent with "expensive, long-duration growth stocks get hit hardest when rates rise" (Unit 1/2 mechanics) rather than any evidence of slowing AI demand itself; worth distinguishing those two stories rather than conflating them. → Route to NR commentary process: plausibly relevant to AI-capex-cycle thesis monitoring; no position-level view expressed here.

META +6.55% (653.69, from 613.48) — what happened: Meta's biggest single-day gain in months, on nearly double its average trading volume. Stated reason: The Motley Fool and Yahoo Finance report Meta launched "Muse," described as a personal AI agent able to shop online, book travel, and manage calendars, with free and paid ($20/$100) tiers; Morgan Stanley was cited estimating the addressable AI-agent market near $30 trillion. Why it matters: an idiosyncratic, company-specific product catalyst that staged a counter-trend rally on a day the S&P fell 0.49% and the Nasdaq fell roughly 0.6% on the rate story above — genuinely different from Vertiv's move the same morning. Read together, Vertiv (infrastructure, sold off on rate/valuation sensitivity) and Meta (application layer, rallied on a product story) show the "AI trade" isn't reacting as one thing right now; no view offered on either stock's investment merit (§8).
chart_of_day_why: The 10-year carries the largest |z| flag on today's board (z +2.14, the highest of any Tier 1 series) after a broad, whole-curve selloff pushed it to 4.83%, its highest close this system has recorded — widely framed in press coverage as a three-year high near 4.85%.
tier3_html:
Daily read: SMH (the semiconductor fund this system uses as an AI-capex proxy) rose 0.10% Wednesday — flat on the day, but that flatness sits on top of a much larger story: SMH is now running roughly 4.7 percentage points ahead of SPY since the 09-02 baseline (directly relevant to CL-0009's expiration and CL-0011, both above). Within the AI-adjacent complex specifically, Wednesday itself showed real dispersion — Vertiv (infrastructure/power) down 9.6% on valuation profit-taking, Meta (application layer) up 6.6% on a product launch (see Movers, above) — a reminder that "AI stocks" isn't one trade right now.

Financing watch: no new hyperscaler or neocloud debt-issuance news surfaced in this morning's search beyond the continued general references to this year's roughly $1.5 trillion in AI-related corporate bond issuance (Bloomberg-sourced, first logged here 09-03) being cited by CNBC and the World Economic Forum as one contributor to this week's broader Treasury-yield pressure — reported as press framing, not confirmed by this system's own data, since this system has no issuance-volume series of its own to test it against (§4C).
calendar_note_html: Today is an event day (§4E): Core PPI m/m (consensus +0.3%) and headline PPI m/m (consensus +0.4%) — both high-impact — print at 8:30am ET, after this morning's data pull, alongside weekly jobless claims (consensus 205K). This brief frames rather than predicts: a hot print would tend to support the inflation/term-premium reading of this week's Treasury selloff (CL-0013, above); an in-line-or-cooler print would tend to support a growth/real-rate or technical (supply, foreign-selling) reading instead. A 30-year bond auction follows at 1:01pm ET — worth watching for a weak bid-to-cover given how much the long end has already moved this week. Tomorrow (Friday) brings the more consequential release: Core CPI y/y (consensus 2.4%, down from 2.5%), the last major inflation print before the Fed's September 15–16 meeting — tomorrow's brief will frame that one in turn, not today's.
concept_title: OAS — the extra yield lenders demand, and why it's a different signal than the level of rates
concept_html: Every bond has a yield, but two things determine it: the "risk-free" Treasury rate (today's whole subject above) and a spread on top, compensating a lender for the chance the borrower doesn't pay them back (default risk) or that the bond is hard to sell quickly without moving its price (liquidity risk). This system tracks that spread using OAS — option-adjusted spread — for both investment-grade (safer, larger companies) and high-yield ("junk," smaller or more leveraged companies) credit. The key idea for today: Treasury yields and credit spreads are two separate dials, not one. Treasury yields mostly reflect Fed policy expectations and how much investors want to be paid for lending money over time (today's whole story). Credit spreads reflect something else — whether lenders are worried about getting paid back at all. Wednesday is about as clean a real-world illustration of that split as this system has recorded: every Treasury tenor flagged as unusually high, while high-yield spreads actually eased and investment-grade spreads didn't move an inch. If today's rate spike reflected real fear about the economy or corporate defaults, credit would typically move first — it's historically the more sensitive, forward-looking gauge of the two. It didn't, which is a big part of why this morning's regime tag reads "tightening" (rates repricing higher) rather than "stress" (the market getting worried about being repaid).
client_translation: "Interest rates jumped again today — the most across-the-board move we've seen since I started sending you these — but the extra yield lenders demand from riskier, junk-rated borrowers barely budged. That gap matters: it's the bond market's way of saying 'borrowing got more expensive for everyone,' not 'we're worried about anyone defaulting.'"
client_lens_html:
• "Rates jumped again — should I be worried?" — The move is real and broad (every Treasury maturity this system tracks is now at an unusually high level for the past six months), so mortgage, CD, and bond-fund pricing are all affected. But the credit market — the piece that would flag actual financial stress — stayed calm, which is the more reassuring half of the story and worth leading with.
  • "Did you see Casey's fall 14% even though earnings beat?" — Yes, and it fits a pattern this system has now tracked three times this cycle (Walmart, Lululemon, now Casey's): strong-but-decelerating growth is getting punished at premium valuations even when the headline numbers are fine, a useful data point on how much slack the market is currently giving consumer-facing names.
  • "Are AI stocks rolling over?" — Mixed signal, and worth being precise about which part of "AI stocks": Vertiv (data-center power/cooling infrastructure) fell nearly 10% on valuation profit-taking the same day Meta jumped 6.6% on a new AI product launch. Not one trade moving together — infrastructure names look more rate-sensitive right now than application-layer names with their own news.
